title: Does UV Light Kill Mold in Air Ducts?
h1: Does UV Light Kill Mold in Air Ducts?
description: UV-C light can kill mold on surfaces it shines on, like the AC coil and drain pan, but it can't reach most duct surfaces. Here's what it does and doesn't do.
quick_answer: UV-C light can kill mold, but only on surfaces it shines on directly and long enough. In an HVAC system, that's mainly the evaporator coil and drain pan near the lamp. It can't reach most of the ductwork, and it won't remove mold that's already growing or fix the moisture problem behind it. Mold in ducts usually needs cleaning plus a moisture fix.
body:
UV light kills mold where it can see it. A UV-C lamp mounted near your AC coil is good at keeping mold from growing on the coil and drain pan, which are the wettest parts of the system. It won't clean mold that's already growing deep in the ducts, because nearly all of the duct interior is out of the lamp's reach.

How does UV-C light kill mold?

UV-C is a short-wavelength ultraviolet light that damages the genetic material in mold, bacteria and viruses, which stops them from growing and reproducing. It takes enough intensity and enough exposure time to work.

That's why placement matters. A lamp that shines on the coil all the time can keep the coil surface clean. A lamp trying to treat air as it rushes past gets only a moment of exposure, so it does much less to spores floating in the airstream.

Where does a UV light work best in an HVAC system?

The best spot is usually inside the air handler or furnace cabinet, aimed at the evaporator coil. The coil gets cold and wet whenever the AC runs, and in coastal homes, damp air from the marine layer keeps it that way for long stretches. Constant UV exposure there helps:

  • Keep mold and biofilm from coating the coil fins
  • Reduce musty smells when the system starts
  • Keep the drain pan cleaner so the condensate line clogs less often
  • Maintain better airflow and heat transfer across the coil

Why can't UV light clear mold from the ducts?

Ducts are long, dark tubes that bend and branch through the attic. Light travels in straight lines, so a lamp in one spot can't reach around corners or down a twenty-foot flex run. Dust on duct walls also shields mold underneath it.

UV light also doesn't remove anything. Even mold it kills stays in place as debris, and dead mold can still irritate allergies. If mold has grown inside the ducts, it needs to be physically cleaned out, and the reason it grew has to be fixed.

What causes mold in air ducts?

Mold needs moisture. In San Diego and Orange County homes, the usual sources are:

  • A clogged condensate drain that lets water back up into the pan or cabinet
  • Uninsulated or poorly insulated ducts in a hot attic that sweat when cold air runs through them
  • Leaky returns pulling in damp air from a crawl space or garage
  • An oversized AC that cools quickly but doesn't run long enough to pull out humidity
  • Roof leaks dripping onto ducts

If the moisture source isn't fixed, mold comes back, with or without a UV light.

What are the signs of mold in your HVAC system?

  • A musty or earthy smell when the AC or heat first turns on
  • Dark spots or fuzzy growth on register covers or around the return grille
  • Water in or around the air handler, or a drain line that keeps clogging
  • Allergy symptoms that flare indoors and ease when you leave home

Dark streaks around ceiling registers aren't always mold. Often they're dust deposits from air leaking around the register boot. A technician can tell the difference and check the coil at the same time.

What's the right way to deal with mold in ducts?

  1. Confirm it. Have a technician inspect the coil, drain pan, blower and ducts. Not every dark spot is mold.
  2. Fix the moisture. Clear the drain, repair duct insulation, seal leaks or address the roof.
  3. Clean the system. Remove contaminated material and clean affected ducts and components. Badly damaged flex duct is usually replaced rather than cleaned.
  4. Prevent it. A UV light at the coil, a good filter and steady humidity control help keep it from returning.

Our indoor air quality technicians install UV lights and can tell you whether your coil is a good candidate. If the ducts need attention, our air duct team handles cleaning and repair.
faqs: Can a UV light replace mold remediation in ducts?
No. UV light can help prevent mold on the coil, but it doesn't remove existing mold from ducts or fix the moisture problem behind it. Active mold needs cleaning and a moisture fix.
Is UV light in an HVAC system safe?

Yes, when installed correctly inside the cabinet or duct, where people can't see the lamp. Never look directly at a UV-C lamp, and turn it off before opening the panel. Many units shut off automatically when the panel is removed.
How long do HVAC UV bulbs last?
Many UV-C bulbs are rated for about a year of continuous use, though output fades before the bulb burns out. Follow the manufacturer's replacement schedule and keep the bulb wiped clean.
